newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel wary of forex market intervention.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel wary of forex market intervention.

text.p: The director of the Bank of Israel's research department said on Sunday the central bank preferred not to intervene in the forex market to stem a further depreciation in the shekel.
"We are following what is happening in the market and now our preference is not to intervene," Leo Leiderman told reporters.
"First of all we have to see how the exchange rate is behaving and then we have to see how the location of the exchange rate within the band affects the inflation environment," he said.
"Not every acceleration of depreciation has to be translated into inflation, especially when we are in a period of economic slowdown and unemployment," Leiderman said.

He said the Bank of Israel would continue to focus on achieving the government's 1997 inflation target of seven to 10 percent. "Our estimate is that the inflation environment right now is at about nine percent," Leiderman said.
The Bank of Israel will recommend next year's target be set at six to nine percent, he added.
Leiderman hinted that if the central bank decides it must take steps to control inflation it would prefer to raise interest rates rather sell foreign currency.
"Our policy is to let the market forces set the exchange rate," he said.
Leiderman said he believes that calm will return to the Israeli forex market soon.

"Our assessment is that...following a certain learning period we'll see fewer fluctuations than what we have seen in the past week," he said. "But we hope there will still be more fluctuations than what we were used to before the change in the exchange rate regime."

The shekel plunged five percent last week after the Israeli cabinet approved exchange rate reform that widened the diagonal band in which the currency may trade, creating more room for a depreciation.
The reform was followed by an interest rate cut of 1.2 percentage points, bringing the central bank's key lending rate to 12.7 percent.

Leiderman said the central bank was committed to defending the upper and lower limit of the band, though market analysts say they believe the central bank will intervene well before the shekel depreciates so far that it reaches the upper band.

"It's still too early to judge the exact level the exchange rate will reach within the band and it's not reasonable to draw conclusions on the basis of developments over one particular day or week. What's more, we are also seeing technical adjustments," Leiderman said.
Many people had sold dollars in advance of the exchange rate measures on expectations of an appreciation of the shekel. Now they are buying back dollars to close positions.

Dealers also said some companies are paying off foreign currency loans to cut their losses. High Israeli interest rates over the past two years had led many in the private sector to take foreign currency loans.

"In our assessment, there are now conditions and potential for a significant drop in short-term capital imports to Israel," Leiderman said, noting domestic interest rates are now well below rates of a year ago and that the trend abroad is towards higher interest rates.
